title: Forty-Seven Years On, the Voyagers Keep Talking
headline: Forty-Seven Years On, the Voyagers Keep Talking
subhead: Launched in 1977 to tour the outer Solar System, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are still sending data from interstellar space — a feat that has outlasted the engineers who built them.
author: Rebecca Hughes
body:
Nearly half a century after leaving Cape Canaveral, the two Voyager spacecraft remain NASA's longest-running mission. Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, and Voyager 2 left sixteen days earlier, on August 20. Both were built at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena.

Their original goal was a grand tour of the outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Voyager 1 reached Jupiter in March 1979, followed by Saturn in November 1980. Voyager 2 took a different path, visiting Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989 before turning toward the outer edge of the Solar System.

The scientific haul from those encounters reshaped planetary science. Voyager 1 discovered active volcanoes on Io, one of Jupiter's moons — the first ever seen beyond Earth. Voyager 2 found that Uranus is tilted on its side and that Neptune has supersonic winds. Both probes captured colour images of Jupiter's Great Red Spot and the thin rings of Saturn with a clarity that earlier missions from Pioneer could not match.

Most famously, in February 1990 Voyager 1 turned its camera backward and took the photograph later known as Pale Blue Dot, showing Earth as a single speck against the darkness. Carl Sagan, who had fought for years to secure the image, wrote about it in his book Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space.

Both craft have now crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun's influence gives way to the interstellar medium. Voyager 1 crossed in August 2012, making it the first human-made object to reach interstellar space. Voyager 2 followed in November 2018. They continue to transmit data on cosmic rays, magnetic fields, and plasma using a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator powered by plutonium-238.

Communication is slow. A signal from Voyager 1, now more than 24 billion kilometres from Earth, takes over 22 hours to reach the Deep Space Network antennas in California, Madrid, and Canberra. Engineers expect the instruments to fall silent by 2030 as the plutonium finally runs out.

Each Voyager also carries a Golden Record — a copper disc of images and sounds selected by a committee led by Sagan. Among them are greetings in fifty-five languages, a child's first words, music by Bach and Chuck Berry, and diagrams of the Solar System showing where the record came from. Neither probe is aimed at any particular star, and neither will come close to one for tens of thousands of years.

For the scientists who still manage the mission from Pasadena, every day brings data no probe has ever returned. As one engineer put it recently, the Voyagers are writing the first chapter of a book about interstellar space that humans have never read.
footer: Reporting by Rebecca Hughes in Pasadena. Additional material from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory archives.
